title: The good I would (Romans 7:15–25)
hook: Paul admits he does what he hates

segments.voice: Yesterday, buried with him in baptism. Your line was newness of life. What did you leave in the water? Day five hundred sixty-four.

New Year's resolution, January first: this year, no more scrolling in bed. January third, one in the morning, the phone glowing on your face. You knew. You meant it. You did it anyway. Almost everyone knows that gap between what we want to do and what we actually do. It's oddly comforting, then, that one of the most important writers in the Christian scriptures describes the same gap, in the first person, with no excuses.
screen: `JANUARY FIRST: A RESOLUTION.` → `JANUARY THIRD, 1 A.M.` → `THE GAP EVERYONE KNOWS.`

segments.voice: In Romans 7, Paul writes, in the King James: "For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I." Would here is the old sense: what I want, what I will. A few lines later he says it again, almost like a man pacing a room: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." He agrees the law is good. He wants the good. And something in him pulls the other way. He calls it sin dwelling in me, a different law at war in his members. And then the cry: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" That's not a theologian's polished sentence. It's a groan. But it doesn't end there. The very next line is: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." The answer isn't a better resolution. It's a person. Now, honesty: Christians have long debated who the I in this chapter is. Some, including Saint Augustine in his later writings, read it as Paul describing his life as a believer, still struggling. Others read it as Paul looking back at life before Christ, or speaking for humanity in Adam's shoes. The Church hasn't required one reading. What Catholics do recognize here is something the tradition calls concupiscence: an inclination toward sin that remains even after baptism, not itself sin, but the place where the struggle happens. Paul doesn't hide it. He names the divided heart, and then he says thank God.
screen: `WHAT I WOULD, THAT DO I NOT.` · `A LAW AT WAR IN MY MEMBERS.` · `O WRETCHED MAN THAT I AM!` · `WHO IS THE I?` · then, large: `I THANK GOD THROUGH JESUS CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest about your divided heart. Settle, and breathe. Name, silently, one thing you keep doing that you don't want to do. Not ten things. One. Don't argue with yourself, don't make a plan yet. Just let it be true, the way Paul let it be true on the page. Notice that naming it is already different from hiding it. Then, if you pray, you can borrow Paul's own words: who shall deliver me, and, I thank God through Jesus Christ. If you don't, simply breathe out, and let the honesty be enough for today. The bell holds the time.
The good I would. Paul's honest confession: the good I want, I don't do, and who shall deliver me? Followed at once by thanks. Today's word.
Your line: who shall deliver me. Today, when you catch yourself in the gap, don't hide it: name it, and ask for help. Day five hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics bring the struggle Paul describes to the sacrament of reconciliation, naming their sins to a priest and receiving absolution, and many make a nightly examination of conscience.

fork.setup: you're writing to a church you've never met, wanting them to trust you. do you admit your own inner struggle?
options: no; present yourself as having it together.
yes; name it plainly, then point to who delivers.
fork.reveal: Paul writes it in the first person: what I hate, that do I. then he names the answer: I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

original.note: Greek: wretched, miserable, worn down. o wretched man that I am.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul was a saint who had it all together.
what it means: he admits in writing that he does what he hates, cries out for deliverance, and thanks God in the next breath.
what a scholar hears: who the I is has been argued since the early Church. Augustine changed his own mind, coming to read it as a believer's struggle; many modern scholars read it differently.
